ai.literal: Learn flawlessly those things worthy of being learned; after learning, stand in accordance with that.
ai.translation: Learn thoroughly and without error what is worthy of being learned; and having learned, let your conduct be worthy of your learning.
ai.modern: கற்க வேண்டியவற்றைத் தங்கு தடையின்றித் தெளிவாகக் கற்க வேண்டும்; அவ்வாறு கற்ற பிறகு, கற்ற கல்விக்கு ஏற்ப நல்வழியில் நடக்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines the complete path of true education. First, one must choose to learn only what is worthy and beneficial. Second, this learning must be done flawlessly (kacaṭaṟa), leaving no room for doubts or errors. Finally, the ultimate test of education is conduct; after learning (kaṟṟapin), one must live and act in perfect alignment (niṟka athaṟkuth thaka) with that knowledge.

ai.literal: Numbers, they say, and the other, letters, they say, these two, eyes, they say, to living beings.
ai.translation: Numbers and letters, these two are said to be the eyes of living beings.
ai.modern: எண் என்றும், மற்றொன்றான எழுத்து என்றும் சொல்லப்படும் இவ்விரண்டையும் வாழ்கின்ற மக்களுக்குக் கண்கள் என்று கூறுவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the fundamental importance of basic education, specifically numeracy and literacy. The poet describes numbers (mathematics) and letters (language and literature) as the two eyes of living human beings. Just as physical eyes are necessary to perceive the physical world, these two disciplines are essential to perceive and understand intellectual and moral truths. Without them, a person remains metaphorically blind despite having physical sight.

ai.literal: Those who possess eyes, they say, are the learned; on the face, two sores possess those who have not learned.
ai.translation: Only those who have acquired learning can be said to possess eyes; those who remain unlearned have merely two sores on their face.
ai.modern: கல்வி கற்றவர்களே கண் உடையவர்கள் என்று சொல்லப்படுவார்கள்; கல்லாதவர்கள் முகத்தில் இரண்டு புண்களை உடையவர்கள் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the transformative power of education by redefining physical sight. The author asserts that true sight belongs only to the educated, who can perceive wisdom, truth, and the deeper realities of life. Conversely, the eyes of the uneducated are dismissed as mere physical cavities or sores on the face, as they lack the inner vision that learning provides. The stark contrast between 'eyes' and 'sores' serves to urge the learner to pursue knowledge.

ai.literal: To meet together so as to delight, and to part so as to be thought of with longing, such is the characteristic nature of the learned.
ai.translation: To meet with delight and to part with a lingering longing to meet again—such is the way of the learned.
ai.modern: மகிழ்ச்சியடையும்படி கூடிப் பேசி, பிரியும்போது மீண்டும் நினைத்துப் பார்க்கும் படியாகப் பிரிவதே கற்றறிந்தவர்களின் இயல்பாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet beautifully defines the nature of intellectual companionship. When scholars meet, their interaction is filled with mutual joy and intellectual stimulation, represented by the word 'uvappa' (to delight). When they part, they do not simply forget each other; instead, they leave a lasting impression that makes them think of and long for each other's company, represented by 'uḷḷa' (to think of with longing). The poet suggests that the ultimate test of a meaningful, learned relationship is that it brings joy in presence and a sweet, reflective longing in absence.

ai.literal: Like those who have nothing before those who possess, even standing in eager humility, those who learned; the lowest indeed are those who have not learned.
ai.translation: Those who acquire learning by standing in eager humility before their teacher, like the destitute standing before the wealthy, are the truly learned; those who do not learn thus are indeed the lowest.
ai.modern: செல்வம் உடையவர்களின் முன் வறியவர்கள் இரந்து நிற்பது போல, பணிந்து நின்று ஏங்கித் தவித்துக் கற்றவர்களே சிறந்தவர்கள்; அவ்வாறு செய்ய நாணி கல்லாதவர் எக்காலத்திலும் கடைப்பட்டவரே ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the necessity of humility in the pursuit of knowledge. The poet compares a student seeking knowledge to a poor person standing expectantly before a wealthy benefactor. Those who are willing to humble themselves and show an eager desire to learn are the ones who become truly educated. Conversely, those who are too proud to adopt this humble posture of learning remain ignorant and are deemed the lowest in society.

ai.literal: To the extent dug, flows the sandy well; to people, to the extent learnt, flows knowledge.
ai.translation: As water flows from a sandy well in proportion to the depth it is dug, so does knowledge flow to people in proportion to the depth of their learning.
ai.modern: தோண்டும் அளவிற்கு மணற்கேணியில் நீர் சுரக்கும்; அதுபோல, கற்கும் அளவிற்கு மக்களுக்கு அறிவு வளரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a beautiful analogy of a sandy well to explain how learning expands the mind. A well dug in sand yields water only as deep as one digs; the deeper you dig, the more water springs forth. Similarly, for human beings, knowledge springs forth and grows only to the extent that they study and learn. The key words 'தொட்டனைத்து' (as much as dug) and 'கற்றனைத்து' (as much as learnt) are perfectly paired to show the direct, proportional relationship between effort and outcome in education.

ai.literal: Any country indeed becomes [his own], any town indeed becomes [his own]; why does a person, until dying, remain without learning?
ai.translation: Since every country and every town becomes a learned person's own, why does anyone remain unlearned until their death?
ai.modern: கற்றவனுக்கு எந்த நாடும் தன் நாடாகும், எந்த ஊரும் தன் ஊராகும்; அப்படியிருக்க, ஒருவன் தன் இறப்பு வரைக்கும் கற்காமல் இருப்பது ஏன்?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the universal acceptance and belonging that education brings to a person. A learned person is welcomed and respected everywhere, making any foreign country or town feel like their own home. Given this immense benefit of learning, which removes all geographical barriers, the poet questions why anyone would choose to remain uneducated throughout their entire life until death. The key words 'nāṭāmāl' (becomes one's country) and 'ūrāmāl' (becomes one's town) emphasize that knowledge grants global citizenship, making the refusal to learn ('kallāta āṟu') highly irrational.

ai.literal: The learning that oneself learned in one birth, to a person, even through seven births, protection it possesses.
ai.translation: The learning that a person acquires in one birth will serve as a protective shield for them throughout all seven of their future births.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் ஒரு பிறவியில் கற்ற கல்வியானது, அவனுக்கு ஏழு பிறவிகளிலும் பாதுகாப்பாக விளங்கும் தன்மை உடையது.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the permanent and transcendent value of education. The word 'ஒருமை' refers to a single lifetime, while 'எழுமை' denotes the concept of seven successive births. The poet explains that the knowledge one acquires ('கற்ற கல்வி') is never lost; instead, it accompanies the soul as a constant source of strength and protection ('ஏமாப்பு') across all future existences. Thus, education is described as the only true wealth that remains with a person eternally.

ai.literal: Themselves that which they enjoy, the world to rejoice having seen, they will desire, those who have learned and known.
ai.translation: Seeing that the world rejoices in the very knowledge that they themselves enjoy, those who have learned and acquired wisdom will desire to learn even more.
ai.modern: தாம் இன்பம் அடையும் கல்வியறிவை உலகமும் பெற்று இன்பமடைவதைக் கண்டு, கற்றறிந்தவர்கள் மேலும் மேலும் கற்க விரும்புவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the profound joy of learning and its social impact. Scholars find personal delight in their own wisdom, but their joy is multiplied when they see the world benefit and rejoice from that same knowledge. The term 'காமுறுவர்' indicates a passionate desire or love, showing that the learned do not grow weary of study; instead, seeing others happy because of their knowledge inspires them to pursue learning even more eagerly.

ai.literal: Ruin-without supreme-wealth learning to-a-person; wealth are-not other those.
ai.translation: Learning is the indestructible, supreme wealth for a person; all other possessions are not true wealth.
ai.modern: ஒருவனுக்கு அழிவில்லாத சிறந்த செல்வம் கல்வியே ஆகும்; அதைத் தவிர மற்றவை எல்லாம் உண்மையான செல்வம் அல்ல.
ai.explanation: This couplet establishes education as the ultimate human possession. The poet describes learning as 'viḻuccelvam' (supreme wealth) because it is 'kēṭil' (without ruin or decay), unlike material riches which can be lost, stolen, or spent. The word 'māṭu' is used here in its classical sense of 'wealth' or 'property'. By declaring that all other things are not true wealth, the verse emphasizes that intellectual and moral growth through education is the only permanent asset a person can acquire.
